It is net authorized capacity: the change in the housing stock if every authorized project is finished. It is not observed stock growth, which needs completion and demolition events by date.

Bound: how many of these a local permit system records, and how many a survey respondent reports as new construction, is unknown. Read the line as the most the reform could add outside the survey definition, not a measured count.
Unavailable: no completion series is read for this state, so no observed completion is reported.
Not modelled: no completion lag is applied, so no permit is turned into a delivered home here. The authorized net change if completed is the upper limit of what these permits could add to the stock.
No mechanism in this reform pushes a permit past 2031; a start delay lowers the total instead (permits not issued are not moved).

The survey covers places that issue building permits; a place with no permit requirement is outside it. The Census Bureau imputes figures for permit offices that did not report, and since 2023 it updates the set of permit offices every year. The baseline projects the published figures, imputations included.

Current law is the law in force on the as-of date. A rule enacted on or before the as-of date with a later effective date is current law from its effective date: when that date falls inside 2027-2031 it is modelled as a reform with a start delay equal to the years between January 1, 2027 and the effective date (the reform's start_delay_years entry), and the run names it. Bills not enacted by the as-of date are scenarios, never baseline. The benchmark reforms are assumed in force on January 1, 2027.

Interest rates, construction costs, rents, home values and household incomes are held at the levels in the ledger and the data packs for the whole window (2027-2031). The baseline repeats recent permit trends under today's rules; it does not predict a recession or a boom. Only the ranges of the ledger entries and the baseline's back-tested range carry uncertainty about them.

New privately owned housing units authorized by building permits, as the Census Bureau's Building Permits Survey counts them, in the five calendar years 2027-2031. A reform's number is the difference from the baseline in the same unit: permits the reform adds, less permits the baseline would have issued anyway on the same sites. The Building Permits Survey leaves out additions, alterations, renovations and conversions of existing buildings, so a unit created that way is not in this measure.

Added units authorized count every new unit that needs a permit. Net added homes subtract the existing homes a project demolishes (the reform's share of them: a demolition that would have happened in the baseline anyway is not the reform's). One house replaced by three homes is three authorizations and two more homes.

What these estimates cannot tell you
These are ranges of building permits, not a forecast of homes finished.
A reform's likely range is a simulation range: it shows how the result moves with the assumptions, given the baseline. No reform of this kind has past totals to check it against.
They describe the whole state. They do not say which lots, streets or owners would build.
They do not say who would live in the new homes or what they would pay.
They assume every town follows the new rule from the first day and approves permits at today's pace.
They say nothing about years after the five-year period.
The baseline repeats recent permit trends under today's rules. It does not predict a recession or a boom.

The baseline range is not a promise. Tested on past years, using only what was known at the time, ranges built this way caught the real five-year total less often than eight times in ten for counties. Each range states how often ranges like it caught the real total.
Those past years hold about one housing cycle, and misses ran mostly to one side and moved together across counties, so the share caught rests on few independent periods.

The rule behind the range was chosen using every past year, including the years it was later scored on, and with today's county types rather than those known at the time, so the share caught is somewhat favourable. Each count's validation card names the study, years and area it comes from.
Counties without a permit office, or with imputed permit counts, carry the Census Bureau's estimates.

The year between the last full year of permit data and the first projected year has no full-year count yet. The baseline carries the latest yearly level through it; a nowcast from the monthly files is shown as a check only, and a part-year count is never treated as a full year.

The middle value depends on which past years the rule averages. In Pennsylvania one unusually high year sits in the window; the baseline card shows the effect of leaving it out as a disclosed sensitivity, not a replacement.

In states with a short permit record, the range is widened toward the past errors of states that grew at a similar pace. Those errors come from one recovery after a housing bust, so the next cycle may differ, and the ranges still caught the real total less often than they aim to.

Where the baseline itself has been least accurate in past years: urban counties (where it has tended to run too low) and counties with a lower share of Qualified Census Tracts (where it has tended to run too low). Read the change in those places with extra care; the Method page shows the back-test.
Whether an ADU fits on a given lot: the fit test is a share for each census tract, not a site plan.
Septic limits, steep slopes, flood zones, historic districts and private deed rules, none of which are in the fit test.
Whether towns slow approvals or add new hurdles.
How quickly owners take up the new right. This is the widest assumption and is not yet checked against places like this state.

Whether every ADU shows up in permit statistics. Many towns permit an ADU as an addition or a conversion, not as a new home, and the national permit survey does not count those, so some of the homes added here may never appear in published permit counts.

Parking near stops is already reduced inside the TOD pro forma (the transit-rich still-built share); the parking reform counts baseline production only, so no unit is counted twice.

Land Massachusetts already zones for multi-family homes by right (Section 3A parcels in the distance, atlas F_L_M__ split across tracts by area) counts only its additional legal capacity: max(0, homes the FAR 2.5 five-storey prototype allows - homes the 3A district already allows) on the same developable land, in gross homes (records existing_3a_*, proposed_3a_capacity, additional_3a_capacity). 3A's 15 homes per acre is a district-wide minimum gross density; the prototype is about 105 per acre on one lot: different measures, so the parcels' own modeled capacity is compared, not the 15-per-acre floor. Eligible land in tracts with no compliant 3A district in the atlas: 53%, existing 3A capacity 0 there (base-zoning rule); the pack cannot tie a tract to its town's 3A status. Variant tod_ma_acre_share keeps the older acre-share rule.

M.G.L. c. 40A § 1A, definition of accessory dwelling unit (St. 2024, c. 150, § 7) (accessory dwelling units)
enacted; effective 2024-08-06; in force on 2026-11-24: not known (no dated record)

An accessory dwelling unit is a self-contained home with its own sleeping, cooking and sanitary space on the same lot as a principal dwelling, with a separate entrance, no larger than half the principal dwelling's gross floor area or 900 square feet, whichever is smaller. A town may add size limits and limit short-term rentals, but may not unreasonably restrict creating or renting an ADU that is not a short-term rental.
M.G.L. c. 40A § 3, ADU paragraph (St. 2024, c. 150, § 8; effective by § 143) (accessory dwelling units)
legally effective; effective 2025-02-02; in force on 2026-11-24

Zoning may not prohibit, unreasonably restrict, or require a special permit or other discretionary approval for one ADU, or renting it, in a single-family residential zoning district. Reasonable rules still apply: Title 5 septic rules (310 CMR 15.000), site plan review, setbacks, bulk and height, and limits on short-term rental. No owner-occupancy requirement. At most one added parking space may be required, and none within 0.5 miles of a commuter rail, subway, ferry or bus station. A second ADU needs a special permit. Against the benchmark: The benchmark allows a detached or semi-detached ADU of at least 600 sq ft with no added parking. The statute already allows one ADU by right in single-family districts; it falls short of the benchmark where the half-of-the-house cap is below 600 sq ft (principal homes under 1,200 sq ft), where a town requires the one parking space (outside 0.5 miles of transit), on single-family lots outside single-family districts, and in Boston, which chapter 40A does not cover. Record ma_adu_by_right_effective (M.G.L. c. 40A § 3, ADU paragraph), verified 2026-11-24. Scope: One ADU (no larger than half the principal home or 900 sq ft) by right in single-family residential zoning districts; at most one added parking space, none within 0.5 miles of a station; no owner-occupancy rule. Exclusions: Boston; a second ADU needs a special permit; Title 5 septic, site plan review, setbacks, bulk, height and short-term-rental limits still apply. Sources: https://malegislature.gov/Laws/GeneralLaws/PartI/TitleVII/Chapter40A/Section3; https://malegislature.gov/Laws/SessionLaws/Acts/2024/Chapter150.
legally effective; effective 2021-01-14; in force on 2026-11-24; court: upheld

Each MBTA community (177 cities and towns; Boston is exempt from chapter 40A) must have at least one zoning district of reasonable size where multi-family housing is allowed as of right, without age limits and suitable for families: a minimum gross density of 15 units per acre and, where applicable, within 0.5 miles of a commuter rail, subway or ferry station or bus station. A community that fails to comply loses eligibility for named state grant programs (Housing Choice, Local Capital Projects, MassWorks, HousingWorks). HLC sets the compliance guidelines (now the regulations 760 CMR 72). Against the benchmark: Close to the transit-oriented density benchmark but narrower: one district per town, sized by HLC's capacity formula, not all land near every stop. Towns choose where the district goes, and most districts are overlays. Districts already adopted and found compliant are in the pack table mbta_3a_districts. Record ma_3a_effective (M.G.L. c. 40A § 3A (St. 2020, c. 358, § 18)), verified 2026-11-24. Scope: The 177 MBTA communities: at least one district of reasonable size with multi-family housing as of right at 15 or more units per acre, within 0.5 miles of a station where applicable. Exclusions: Boston (not subject to chapter 40A). Sources: https://malegislature.gov/Laws/GeneralLaws/PartI/TitleVII/Chapter40A/Section3A; https://malegislature.gov/Laws/SessionLaws/Acts/2020/Chapter358.

The flood share uses FEMA's regulatory 1% annual chance floodplain; it leaves out heavy-rain flooding away from mapped streams, and some flood maps are decades old. Groups and neighbours describe how alike places are on a few published numbers (population, growth, density, rents, home values, building, transit, renters, empty homes, age); they say nothing about why. U.S. Census Bureau, Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics program

Counts jobs covered by unemployment insurance plus federal civilian jobs, by where people work. Self-employed people, the military and informal work are not counted. Links each job's workplace block to the worker's home block. The "main" file covers jobs with both ends in the state; the "aux" file adds workers who live in another state. Residents who work in another state are in that state's files, which are not read, so out-commuting across the state line is not counted. Same job coverage as the workplace file.

Counts private establishments with paid employees and their mid-March employment and yearly payroll. Government, self-employed and most farm work are left out.
